newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria banks eye new investment alternatives.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria banks eye new investment alternatives.

text.p: The introduction of a fixed exchange rate regime has prompted Bulgarian banks to seek investment alternatives to the narrowing local foreign exchange market, traders said on Wednesday.

"Since the lev was pegged to the mark, foreign currency investments and operations on the local forex market are no longer profitable and we are now seeking better investment opportunities," said Bisser Manolov, chief dealer at Bulbank, the Bulgarian foreign trade bank.

Under the currency board arrangement, the central bank has pledged to exchange unlimited amounts of marks for levs at a fixed exchange rate with a bid level of 995 levs per mark and an asking level of 1,000 levs.
"The low interest rate and fixed exchange rate are bad news for forex speculators, but banks now can resort to creative lending," one resident banker said.
The lev traded on Wednesday close to central bank ranges at 994-995.30 per mark on a quiet interbank market, dealers said.

The currently available investment alternatives are interbank lev deposits, bad loan bonds issued by the government to cover non-performing loans issued by local banks, and Bulgarian Brady bonds issued to restructure an $8.16 billion commercial debt three years ago.
Banks are also focusing more on arbitrage deals on international money markets, traders said.
Secondary trade on the domestic treasury market has been very thin after a recent fall of interest rates due to excessive lev liquidity in the banking system.
The T-bill issues offered at primary auctions have been heavily oversubscribed which led to a sharp decrease in their yields.
The average yield to maturity of the three-month discount T-bills offered by the Finance Ministry on Monday fell to 2.46 percent from 2.55 percent for the respective maturity traded on June 23.

"With such high liquidity most banks are on the buyer side at the secondary market, which makes trade extremely thin. Interbank deposit trade is also almost non-existent at the moment due to the low demand for funds," another trader said.
The banks are also selling some of their foreign currency bought before the introduction of the currency board at higher lev rates, to gain from the lower lev peg.
Once the stock market is revived later this year, it will provide additional investment alternatives, traders said.
"Creditworthiness of the banks has yet to be evaluated and most banks still do not have account limits with each other to step up options and futures trade," said a dealer.
Many of the traders have yet to be trained in derivative trading, the dealer added.
